title: Discovery of the Parts of the Atom: Electrons and Nuclei
lead: The electron and the nucleus were found by experiments that use the electric and magnetic forces of earlier chapters. Thomson bent beams of cathode rays, Millikan held charged drops of oil still between metal plates, and Rutherford fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil, and their results lead to the planetary model of the atom.
objectives: Explain the Millikan oil drop experiment.
Describe Rutherford’s planetary model of the atom.
summary_html:
• Atoms are composed of negatively charged electrons, first proved to exist in cathode-ray-tube experiments, and a positively charged nucleus.
  • All electrons are identical and have a charge-to-mass ratio of$$\frac{\kqe}{\kme}=-1.76\times 10^{11}\;\text{C/kg.}$$
  • The positive charge in the nuclei is carried by particles called protons, which have a charge-to-mass ratio of$$\frac{\kqp}{\kmp}=9.57\times 10^{7}\;\text{C/kg.}$$
  • Mass of electron,$$\kme=9.11\times 10^{-31}\;\text{kg.}$$
  • Mass of proton,$$\kmp=1.67\times 10^{-27}\;\text{kg.}$$
  • The planetary model of the atom pictures electrons orbiting the nucleus in the same way that planets orbit the sun.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 30.6) Diagram of Thomson’s CRT. (credit: Kurzon, Wikimedia Commons) (Figure 30.7) This schematic shows the electron beam in a CRT passing through crossed electric and magnetic fields and causing phosphor to glow when striking the end of the tube.

The Millikan oil drop experiment produced the first accurate direct measurement of the charge on electrons, one of the most fundamental constants in nature. Fine drops of oil become charged when sprayed. Their movement is observed between metal plates with a potential applied to oppose the gravitational force. The balance of gravitational and electric forces allows the calculation of the charge on a drop. The charge is found to be quantized in units of −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, thus determining directly the charge of the excess and missing electrons on the oil drops.

(Figure 30.10) Rutherford’s experiment gave direct evidence for the size and mass of the nucleus by scattering alpha particles from a thin gold foil. Alpha particles with energies of about 5 MeV are emitted from a radioactive source (which is a small metal container in which a specific amount of a radioactive material is sealed), are collimated into a beam, and fall upon the foil. The number of particles that penetrate the foil or scatter to various angles indicates that gold nuclei are very small and contain nearly all of the gold atom’s mass. This is particularly indicated by the alpha particles that scatter to very large angles, much like a soccer ball bouncing off a goalie’s head. (Figure 30.11) An expanded view of the atoms in the gold foil in Rutherford’s experiment. Circles represent the atoms (about 10⁻¹⁰ m in diameter), while the dots represent the nuclei (about 10⁻¹⁵ m in diameter). To be visible, the dots are much larger than scale. Most alpha particles crash through but are relatively unaffected because of their high energy and the electron’s small mass. Some, however, head straight toward a nucleus and are scattered straight back. A detailed analysis gives the size and mass of the nucleus.

Rutherford’s planetary model of the atom incorporates the characteristics of the nucleus, electrons, and the size of the atom. This model was the first to recognize the structure of atoms, in which low-mass electrons orbit a very small, massive nucleus in orbits much larger than the nucleus. The atom is mostly empty and is analogous to our planetary system.

exercises.prompt:
In an experiment, three microscopic latex spheres are sprayed into a chamber and become charged with +3e, +5e, and −3e, respectively. Later, all three spheres collide simultaneously and then separate. Which of the following are possible values for the final charges on the spheres? Select two answers.
  1. +4e, −4e, +5e
  2. −4e, +4.5e, +4.5e
  3. +5e, −8e, +7e
  4. +6e, +6e, −7e

In Millikan’s oil drop experiment, he experimented with various voltage differences between two plates to determine what voltage was necessary to hold a drop motionless. He deduced that the charge on the oil drop could be found by setting the gravitational force on the drop (pointing downward) equal to the electric force (pointing upward): $\kmdrop\kg=\kq\kEf$, where $\kmdrop$ is the mass of the oil drop, $\kg$ is the gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s²), $\kq$ is the net charge of the oil drop, and $\kEf$ is the electric field between the plates. Millikan deduced that the charge on an electron, e, is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. For a system of oil drops of equal mass (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ kilograms), describe what value or values of the electric field would hold the drops motionless.

answer.solution: Solve the balance for the field, $\kEf = \kmdrop\kg/\kq$. Every drop has the same mass, so the field that holds a drop depends only on its charge. Millikan found that the charge on a drop is always a whole number of electron charges, $\kq = Ne$ with $N = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$, so there is not one field but a set of them, $\kEf = \kmdrop\kg/(Ne)$. Work out the largest, for a drop carrying a single extra electron; every other field that holds a drop is that value divided by a whole number, and no field in between holds any drop still.

exercises.prompt:
What two pieces of evidence allowed the first calculation of $\kme$, the mass of the electron?
  1. The ratios $\kqe/\kme$ and $\kqp/\kmp$.
  2. The values of $\kqe$ and $E_{B}$.
  3. The ratio $\kqe/\kme$ and $\kqe$.
Justify your response.

answer.solution: Ask what each experiment measured. Thomson’s crossed fields gave the ratio $\kqe/\kme$ but neither quantity alone, and Millikan’s oil drops gave the charge $\kqe$ itself. Dividing the charge by the ratio, $\kme = \kqe/(\kqe/\kme)$, gives the mass, which is choice (c). The two ratios of choice (a) only compare the electron with the proton and cannot give either mass on its own.

exercises.prompt: Rutherford found the size of the nucleus to be about $10^{-15}\;\text{m}$. This implied a huge density. What would this density be for gold?

answer.hint: Take the gold nucleus to be a sphere $10^{-15}$ m across that holds nearly all the mass of a gold atom, 197 u.

exercises.prompt:
(a) An aspiring physicist wants to build a scale model of a hydrogen atom for her science fair project. If the atom is 1.00 m in diameter, how big should she try to make the nucleus?

(b) How easy will this be to do?

answer.hint: The nucleus is about $10^{-15}$ m across and the atom about $10^{-10}$ m, so the nucleus is 100,000 times smaller.
answer.solution:
(a) $10.0\;\mu\text{m}$

(b) It isn’t hard to make one of approximately this size. It would be harder to make it exactly $10.0\;\mu\text{m}$.

exercises.prompt: Using the given charge-to-mass ratios for electrons and protons, and knowing the magnitudes of their charges are equal, what is the ratio of the proton’s mass to the electron’s? (Note that since the charge-to-mass ratios are given to only three-digit accuracy, your answer may differ from the accepted ratio in the fourth digit.)

answer.hint: With $|\kqp| = |\kqe|$, the ratio of the masses is the inverse of the ratio of the charge-to-mass ratios.

exercises.prompt: If someone wanted to build a scale model of the atom with a nucleus 1.00 m in diameter, how far away would the nearest electron need to be?

answer.hint: The atom is about $10^{-10}$ m across and its nucleus about $10^{-15}$ m, 100,000 times smaller; the nearest electron is about the atom’s radius from the nucleus.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts The electric and magnetic forces on an electron in the CRT in Figure 30.7 are supposed to be in opposite directions. Verify this by determining the direction of each force for the situation shown. Explain how you obtain the directions (that is, identify the rules used).

answer.solution: The electric force on the electron is up (toward the positively charged plate). The magnetic force is down (by the RHR).

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts In a Millikan oil-drop experiment using a setup like that in Figure 30.9, a 500-V potential difference is applied to plates separated by 2.50 cm. (a) What is the mass of an oil drop having two extra electrons that is suspended motionless by the field between the plates? (b) What is the diameter of the drop, assuming it is a sphere with the density of olive oil?

parts.hint: Divide the mass by the density of olive oil, 920 kg/m³, to get the volume, then find the diameter of a sphere of that volume.

exercises.prompt: Integrated Concepts In a laboratory experiment designed to duplicate Thomson’s determination of $\kqe/\kme$, a beam of electrons having a velocity of $6.00\times 10^{7}\;\text{m/s}$ enters a $5.00\times 10^{-3}\;\text{T}$ magnetic field. The beam moves perpendicular to the field in a path having a 6.80-cm radius of curvature. Determine $\kqe/\kme$ from these observations, and compare the result with the known value.

answer.hint: The magnetic force is the centripetal force, $|\kqe|\kv\kBmag = \kme\kv^2/r$, so $|\kqe|/\kme = \kv/(r\kBmag)$.
answer.solution: $1.76\times 10^{11}\;\text{C/kg}$, which agrees with the known value of $1.759\times 10^{11}\;\text{C/kg}$ to within the precision of the measurement

referents.label: the oil drop held between the plates
